hpi_details: 62-year-old female referred for resistant hypertension despite being on 3 maximum-dose antihypertensive medications (Amlodipine, Lisinopril, HCTZ). Routine labs showed persistent unprovoked hypokalemia (K 2.9). Reports occasional muscle weakness and cramps.
ideas: She thinks her body has built up a tolerance to her current blood pressure pills, and that the leg cramps are just from not eating enough bananas.
concerns: She is worried that her persistently sky-high blood pressure will cause a sudden stroke and leave her paralyzed like her older sister.
expectations: She hopes the doctor can switch her to a more effective blood pressure medication and provide a supplement to relieve her muscle cramps.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Primary Aldosteronism is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Screening begins with aldosterone-to-renin ratio after potassium correction and attention to interfering medicines; mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists such as spironolactone should be started after diagnostic testing or used when testing cannot be completed.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: resistant hypertension and hypokalemia

Key HPI features: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with resistant hypertension and hypokalemia. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Primary Aldosteronism.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Primary Aldosteronism.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Renal artery stenosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe weakness.
management_principles: Correct hypokalemia and obtain an aldosterone-to-renin ratio with appropriate medication management; confirm and subtype disease before selecting surgery or mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist therapy
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Aldosteronism — Case Detection, Diagnosis, and Treatment

reference_soap.subjective: 62-year-old female referred for resistant hypertension despite being on 3 maximum-dose antihypertensive medications (Amlodipine, Lisinopril, HCTZ). Routine labs showed persistent unprovoked hypokalemia (K 2.9). Reports occasional muscle weakness and cramps.
reference_soap.objective: BP 168/95. Heart rate 82. Exam is generally unremarkable. No abdominal bruits. Labs show K+ 2.9 mEq/L, metabolic alkalosis.
reference_soap.plan: Check plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) and plasma renin activity (PRA) ratio. Withhold interfering anti-hypertensives (e.g., switch to Verapamil/Doxazosin) prior to testing. Replete potassium. Consider adrenal CT if ratio is high.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Primary Aldosteronism
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Primary Aldosteronism
Implement evidence-based management plan: Correct potassium, screen with aldosterone-to-renin ratio using appropriate medication management, then confirm and subtype disease before treatment

teaching.one_liner: An aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma causing resistant hypertension and hypokalemia.

must_ask.say: How hard is your blood pressure to control?
How long has this been going on?
What blood pressure medications are you on?

history.answer: I came in because my blood pressure stays high even though I take three different blood pressure pills every single day.
My doctor told me my blood pressure was still over 160, and my routine blood test showed that my potassium was unusually low.
My blood pressure has been creeping up over the past year despite adding more pills, but this is the first time my potassium came back low.
I had fasted overnight before the blood draw, sat quietly for fifteen minutes before the pressure was checked, and had no morning coffee.
I check it every morning and evening at home, and it consistently runs around 165 over 95.
My blood pressure started resisting medications about six months ago, and over the past month I've felt noticeably more fatigued.
I've been getting painful muscle cramps in my calves at night and occasional weak spells in my legs.
I've been feeling thirstier than usual, and I now have to wake up two or three times every night to urinate.
I get mild dull headaches in the back of my head occasionally, but no lightheadedness or spinning sensation.
No, I haven't had any chest pressure, shortness of breath, sudden blurry vision, or weakness on one side of my body.
No, I have never had kidney stones, severe back pain, or persistent bone aches.
I haven't had any fevers, night sweats, unexpected weight loss, or swollen glands.
I don't get pounding heart palpitations, drenching sweat episodes, or loud snoring at night.
I don't use pain relievers like ibuprofen, steroid creams or pills, nasal decongestants, or real licorice candy.
I cook with very little salt, avoid processed food, and take a brisk thirty-minute walk three days a week.
I went through menopause around age fifty-one, and I have never broken any bones or lost height.
I have never had tuberculosis, never been around anyone with it, and do not take immune-suppressing drugs.
I assumed my body became immune to my blood pressure pills, and that the leg cramps were just because I need to eat more bananas.
I'm terrified that with my numbers this high despite all these pills, I'm going to have a massive stroke just like my sister did.
I hope you can switch me to a different blood pressure pill that actually works and give me a supplement for these painful muscle cramps.
I was diagnosed with high blood pressure about eight years ago, but it only became difficult to control within the last two years.
I had an uncomplicated appendectomy in my twenties, but I have never been hospitalized since then.
I take amlodipine 10 milligrams, lisinopril 40 milligrams, and hydrochlorothiazide 25 milligrams every morning without missing doses.
I only take a daily women's multivitamin and an occasional acetaminophen for mild headaches.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I drink socially, maybe one glass of red wine every couple of weeks when I go out.
I am a retired high school administrative assistant living with my husband in a single-story home.
My mother had high blood pressure in her late sixties, but no one in my family had strokes, heart attacks, or kidney failure at a young age.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 168/95 mmHg, heart rate is 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.
Well-nourished, alert female in no acute distress, with normal facial features and no moon facies, buffalo hump, or abdominal striae.
No arteriolar narrowing, cotton wool spots, flame hemorrhages, or papilledema on funduscopic examination.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, mobile, with no palpable nodules or bruits.
No palpable anterior or posterior cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2, without murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Normoactive bowel sounds present; no epigastric, renal artery, or femoral bruits heard.
Soft, non-tender, non-distended, with no palpable masses or hepatosplenomegaly.
Normal spinal alignment without kyphosis, scoliosis, or midline vertebral tenderness.
Bilateral radial, femoral, and dorsalis pedis pulses are 2+, symmetrical, and synchronous without radiofemoral delay.
No pretibial or pedal edema bilaterally.
Motor strength is 5/5 throughout the upper and lower extremities with normal tone.
